strengths: The paper tackles an important practical bottleneck in diffusion-based image super-resolution: reducing ResShift-style restoration to one inference step while preserving perceptual quality and fidelity.

The proposed RSD objective is technically interesting, connecting ResShift distillation to an auxiliary fake model and trajectory-level distribution matching. The manuscript provides derivations, pseudocode, and comparisons to VSD, ADD/AddSR, SiD, FGM, and IBMD.

The experimental coverage is broad: RealSR, RealSet65, DRealSR, ImageNet-Test, DIV2K crops, full-size and cropped settings, plus comparisons to ResShift, SinSR, OSEDiff, SUPIR, GAN-based methods, transformer baselines, VSD, and AddSR.

The efficiency results are compelling for the target niche: RSD keeps the compact ResShift/SinSR-scale architecture, one-step inference, low memory, and much lower parameter count than T2I-based SR systems.
The appendix includes useful implementation details, hyperparameters, dataset/model provenance, ablations, failure cases, limitations, and a societal impact discussion.
weaknesses: The central theoretical motivation is not fully convincing. The assumption that a fake ResShift model matching the teacher implies the generated LR-HR joint distribution matches real data is strong and not identifiable in general; many data distributions can induce similar predictors. The equivalence also relies on exact optimization of the auxiliary fake model, whereas the actual method uses alternating finite updates.

The claimed advantage over VSD/ADD is partly conceptual but not conclusively isolated experimentally. The final method combines the proposed distillation with LPIPS and GAN losses, and the ablations show these supervised/adversarial losses substantially change the trade-off; it remains hard to attribute gains cleanly to the new RSD objective.

The strongest claims about perceptual realism and reduced hallucination are supported mostly by no-reference IQA metrics and selected visual examples. For super-resolution, these metrics can reward hallucinated texture, so the absence of a human preference study or task-based fidelity evaluation weakens the evidence.

Results are good but not uniformly state of the art. RSD often improves over SinSR and is attractive for compact one-step inference, but OSEDiff/SUPIR/SeeSR/PASD or even GAN/transformer baselines outperform it on several datasets and metrics, especially fidelity or some no-reference metrics. The headline “outperforms the teacher by a large margin” needs qualification because it often trades PSNR/SSIM for perceptual scores.

Reproducibility is moderate rather than strong. The paper gives pseudocode, hyperparameters, and baseline sources, but I did not see a commitment to release RSD code, checkpoints, training scripts, or exact evaluation outputs. Several baselines are borrowed from prior papers while others are rerun, which can introduce comparability issues.

Presentation is generally clear, but the paper is lengthy and occasionally overclaims relative to the evidence. There are also minor typos and awkward formulations, and some key claims are deferred to dense appendices rather than being crisply justified in the main text.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing diffusion-based super-resolution to one inference step while retaining perceptual quality and lower memory/parameter cost than large text-to-image SR systems.

The submission includes a fairly broad empirical suite across RealSR, RealSet65, DRealSR, ImageNet-Test, and DIV2K-style crops, and compares against ResShift, SinSR, OSEDiff, SUPIR, GAN, and transformer baselines in the appendix.

The proposed method is computationally attractive relative to T2I-based SR models: the reported inference time and memory are close to SinSR and far below SUPIR/OSEDiff, while often improving no-reference perceptual metrics over ResShift/SinSR.
The paper provides useful implementation detail, pseudocode, ablations for multistep training and supervised losses, failure cases, dataset/license tables, and an LLM-use statement.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification is not sound enough to support the claims. The paper assumes that if a ResShift model trained on generated outputs coincides with the teacher, then the generated LR-HR distribution matches the data distribution. This is a very strong identifiability assumption and is not established; matching an MSE-trained denoiser/conditional expectation need not determine the full conditional image distribution, especially for a stochastic generator.

The claimed equivalence to a joint KL objective is questionable and appears to conflate distributions induced by the learned reverse process with tractable forward noising distributions over generator samples. Even if the algebra in Proposition 3.1 holds under idealized optimal fake-model assumptions, the implemented alternating finite-capacity fake model does not justify the stronger distribution-matching conclusions.

The experimental evidence is mixed and the paper overclaims. Statements such as outperforming the teacher by a large margin are mainly true for selected perceptual/no-reference metrics, while fidelity metrics often drop versus ResShift/SinSR. In extended tables, simple GAN/transformer baselines sometimes beat RSD on PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, or NIQE; these results are downplayed relative to favorable no-reference metrics.

The evaluation relies heavily on CLIPIQA and MUSIQ for perceptual claims without human preference studies or task-based validation. This is problematic in super-resolution, where no-reference IQA can reward hallucinated texture and may not reflect faithfulness to the LR input.

Comparisons to recent one-step/distillation SR methods are incomplete. The paper cites TSD-SR, AddSR, CCSR-related concerns, etc., but the main empirical comparison is largely against SinSR, OSEDiff, SUPIR, and an in-house ResShift-VSD variant. The AddSR comparison is relegated to the appendix and is confounded by architecture/training differences.

The fairness of some comparisons is not fully convincing: RSD is trained under the ResShift/SinSR setup while OSEDiff/SUPIR use different priors, data, crop sizes, and sometimes proprietary or larger datasets. The appendix partially explores 512x512 training, but the results then show RSD still lags OSEDiff on no-reference perceptual quality.

Ablations do not isolate the proposed distillation objective cleanly enough. The final method includes LPIPS and GAN losses, and the reported ablation shows these supervised/adversarial terms materially change PSNR/LPIPS and no-reference scores, making it hard to attribute gains to the new RSD objective.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Hyperparameters, pseudocode, datasets, and baseline sources are described, but there is no clear code/model release commitment in the manuscript, and reproducing the results would require multiple external repositories/checkpoints and nontrivial engineering.

The limitations and societal-impact section is present but shallow. It acknowledges hallucinations and misuse/deepfake risks, but the risk argument that ImageNet-only training implies low misuse risk is not well substantiated for a generative restoration model that may fabricate details.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing diffusion-based real-world super-resolution to one inference step while retaining perceptual quality and input fidelity. The motivation is clear, especially the gap between efficient ResShift/SinSR-style models and heavier T2I-based methods such as OSEDiff and SUPIR.

The proposed RSD objective is technically interesting. Framing distillation as training the student so that a fake ResShift model trained on student outputs matches the teacher is a useful adaptation of distribution-matching/fake-model distillation ideas to the residual-shift SR setting. The manuscript also gives a reasonably detailed derivation and positions the objective against VSD, SDS/ADD, SiD/FGM, and IBMD.

The empirical evaluation is broad and mostly convincing. Results cover real-world and synthetic datasets including RealSR, RealSet65, DRealSR, ImageNet-Test, and DIV2K/StableSR crops. RSD consistently improves over SinSR on perceptual metrics and is competitive with OSEDiff/SUPIR while using far fewer parameters, memory, and inference steps.

The ablations are useful. The multistep-training and supervised-loss studies clarify which design choices affect the perception-distortion tradeoff, and the ResShift-VSD baseline helps isolate the proposed loss from a straightforward VSD adaptation.

The appendix contains substantial reproducibility detail, including pseudocode, training time, optimizer settings, loss weights, dataset/model sources, licenses, additional baselines, higher-resolution training results, AddSR comparison, limitations, failure cases, societal impact, and LLM usage.
weaknesses: The central theoretical motivation still depends on a strong assumption: if a fake ResShift trained on generated outputs matches the teacher, then the generated LR-HR distribution matches the data distribution. This is plausible but not fully justified, especially because equality or closeness of learned denoisers need not uniquely identify the underlying conditional image distribution in practical finite-capacity settings.

The empirical claims rely heavily on automatic perceptual and no-reference metrics such as CLIPIQA, MUSIQ, MANIQA, NIQE, LPIPS, and DISTS. For a paper making claims about hallucination, realism, and fidelity tradeoffs, a human preference/user study or stronger diagnostic hallucination/fidelity analysis would substantially strengthen the evidence.

Some comparisons are not perfectly controlled. OSEDiff and SUPIR use different training data, model classes, crop sizes, and priors; the authors discuss this, and the 512x512 appendix helps, but the main conclusions about matching T2I-based methods remain somewhat conditional on these setup differences.

Reproducibility is decent but not complete. The paper says it builds on SinSR and gives many details, but some hyperparameters are inherited by reference rather than fully restated, random seed/statistical variability is not reported, and there is no clear statement that code and trained weights will be released.

The novelty is meaningful but incremental relative to recent distribution-matching distillation methods. The paper’s own appendix shows close connections to VSD, SiD/FGM, and IBMD; the main originality is a careful SR-specific adaptation and empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new distillation paradigm.

The societal-impact discussion is present but somewhat too dismissive: saying misuse risk is low because the model is trained on ImageNet does not fully address applications of super-resolution to surveillance, forensic misuse, synthetic evidence, or biased restoration of faces and sensitive imagery.
